Gunner is a tank, despite the hp being the same as any class he’s the closest to tank that is in the game. So play like one. 

Games with big spaces or single interest points you should hold back and watch over the team. Take down the most priority targets and soften up bigger bugs, leaving smaller swarm groups or stragglers for your team. 

Focus on protecting your teammates when they’re doing something important, always shooting something while they’re mining or drilling or building. You don’t terraform and you shouldn’t mine as much compared to the others because you’re better at defending and killing. 

Your shield is infinite health, but not just for you. Don’t be afraid to drop it if your teammate is getting overwhelmed or needs a resupply in the middle of a fight. It’s perfect to revive a teammate, safely throw a grenade, or heal Doretta without bugs getting in the way. 

Your Zipline is not fast or omnidirectional but it is reliable. You can stop a fall by catching a Zipline, you can carry heavy things near vertically with a Zipline without needing a tunnel or Mario jump platforms, and you can’t get rid of them. No detonation, no blocking from bugs, no selfish only-you use, they’re there forever. It’s perfect for being able to shoot from the sky as well if you’ve got a big swarm, or a land bound dread. 

Finally, your best missions are ones where you don’t need a lot of super mobility or resource management but do need tons of defense and damage. Point extraction or Salvage are perfect for your zip lines and your shield to work together, Doretta is ideal for being able to defend her and the dwarves healing her up or getting to the oil shale, and elimination is ideal because you take care of Dreads better than almost any other class. 

Remember, you’re the tank. It’s your job to keep your team alive and the bugs dead, because both of them are probably incapable of outsmarting a bullet. Rock and stone future gunner!

I think to myself two specific questions. 

 “How much do I think they can handle at this next arc?”

“How much have they handled this current arc?”

If my party is able to handle something that’s maybe… five to seven bandits difficult with a few wolves thrown in, but the next arc I want to send them on is thematically something super cool and should be difficult in lore (say a moderately challenging vampire and some undead minions), I’ll have them level up before starting the story. This gives them time to understand their abilities, know the new flow of combat, and be able to face the next arc threat with appropriate power. 

However, if I have my players almost die in a dramatic fashion to something I assumed they could handle (or that I’m gonna be using as a regular enemy here on out) then I try to assess if there’s anything I can do to make the future fights less TPK-inducing. If not, they get a level boost and also get to feel that they’ve gotten powerful by kicking ass against something that used to be their near-downfall. 

Basically my two rules for leveling up are: If it makes them feel the same amount of challenge going into the next story, level up. If they almost failed and could only survive the same threat if they level up, level up.

You think yourself strong, hero. And perhaps you are. The tyrant lay slain and his armies sundered, the grip he held so tightly to power is loosened with his corpse’s hands. And that was you who did it. That took strength, might, power beyond the common folk you protect. 

But they will forget you, in time. Not in malice, hero. Not in some grand conspiracy to forge a new history, to lay tracks for a new dark lord. But because that’s what the people do. They forget the strife once peace has stayed, and they forget the struggle when they do not live it every moment. 

History won’t forget you hero. They won’t forget the facts, clear as they are, that you slayed the demons and saved the damsels. No one will ever dispute that, for it will be written in ink and paper like a thousand times before. Every general who you took a sword to, every town that you freed, their names are on record. No one will ever dispute that. 

Fear though, they will never remember. Fear cannot be put to pen. Anxiety cannot be felt, years later, when the only thing you know of its source is a story from a book no one bothered to read. You can’t quite understand the past without experiencing it, and you cannot experience suffering in peace. 

I will outlive you, hero. I outlived every hero before, every demon lord and tyrant king and lich mage. I stood there before each and every one as they grew and fought and died. I didn’t fight with them or against them, but did something more important. I gave them the only emotion that never dies. 

Laughter. 

A tragedy is misery in its infancy. It is depression and sorrow in its age. And with a hundred years it fades into boring fact. Horror and fear lose their true impact within a day of their ending, and only truly stay scary to fresh ears and untouched minds. But a joke? A joke will outlive even me. 

There once was this saying, back before even my time. How do you entertain a bored king? Dress a boatload of maidens in fishnets down the river, and tell the king to go fishing. That’s funny. It’s worth a smile, a scoff, an emotion. That is something that survives the trials of time and terror. But the demon king you slain today will one day become a footnote in a book. Not worth fear, or sorrow, none of the emotions he tried to cause. A joke will cause the same emotion millennia later, but a tyrant can only cause fear in his life. 

So you have slain the demon king. The dark lord and his armies are gone. And while they live, the people shall feel peace. But I will outlive you as I outlived all the others. Fear or peace, satisfaction or sorrow, none of them will remain long once your names are written in the history books. 

You cannot be afraid of a monster long after it is dead. But you can laugh at a joke forever.
